analysis.one_liner: Blocks app store owners from forcing developers into their payment systems and favoring their own apps.
analysis.headline: The Open App Markets Act was introduced in the House in August 2021 with a bipartisan sponsor team but never got a committee hearing or a vote, and it died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set rules for app stores run by companies with more than 50 million U.S. users — in practice Apple and Google. It would bar them from forcing app developers to use their in-house payment systems, from punishing developers who offer cheaper pricing elsewhere, from using developers' private data to build competing products, and from ranking their own apps above rivals in search results. It also would have let users install apps from other stores and let developers sue for triple damages if they were harmed.
analysis.who_benefits: App developers, especially small and mid-sized ones, who currently pay up to 30% commissions to Apple's and Google's app stores on many transactions. Consumers benefit indirectly through lower app prices, more choice, and the ability to install apps and app stores outside Apple's and Google's official storefronts. Both FTC and DOJ enforcement and private lawsuits by injured developers would police the rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small app developers and app users

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits an app store owner from requiring developers to use its own payment system as a condition of distribution, and from punishing developers who use or offer different pricing elsewhere [S3].

Bars the store owner from using non-public business information collected from third-party apps to compete with those apps, and from unreasonably ranking its own or its partners' apps above rivals [S3].
Requires the store owner to let users choose third-party apps and app stores as defaults, install apps outside its store, and delete preinstalled apps [S3].
Gives injured developers the right to sue in federal court for threefold damages plus attorney's fees, and lets the FTC, the Justice Department, and state attorneys general enforce the rules [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Apple and Google, the two companies whose app stores each serve far more than 50 million U.S. users, would lose a large stream of commission revenue and the gatekeeping control over which apps users can install and how they pay. Developers who benefit from store placement protections would face no direct cost, though the companies could pass some compliance costs along.
analysis.who_pays_short: Apple and Google's app store businesses

drawbacks.text: Apple and Google argue their tight control of app distribution and payments is a privacy and security feature, and loosening it could expose users to more fraud and malware; the bill responds with a safe harbor for actions genuinely needed for privacy, security, or fraud prevention, but only if the company proves the action is consistently applied and narrowly tailored [S3].

Companies above the 50-million-user threshold would face detailed federal regulation of app ranking, payment terms, and software defaults, which critics of such legislation warn could invite litigation and regulatory second-guessing of platform design decisions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a specific, widely felt cost: app store commissions and gatekeeping that raise prices for consumers and squeeze small developers. The strongest objection — that loosening store control could weaken security — is addressed, though not eliminated, by a safe harbor that puts the burden on the store owner to prove its restrictions are real and even-handed. On balance the benefits for developers and consumers outweigh the compliance costs, which fall on two of the most profitable companies in the country.

outcome.mechanism: The House bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the two-year Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Hank Johnson (D-GA) introduced the bill on August 13, 2021, joined by Representatives Buck and Cicilline, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S5].
The bill's only action was that referral; no hearing, markup, or floor vote is recorded, and it died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].
The bill attracted seven cosponsors, one Republican and six Democrats [S4].
The Senate companion bill, which a Senate committee advanced, was not among the provided sources for this House bill; the House version itself never advanced past referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Apple and Google are better off because the bill never got a vote: they keep their app store commission structures and control over app distribution without facing the payment, self-preferencing, and sideloading mandates the bill would have imposed. Developers and consumers gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced with one Republican and two Democratic original sponsors and drew seven cosponsors split 1 Republican and 6 Democrats, but it never reached a vote where party splits could be measured.

industries.note: The bill would bar both companies from requiring developers to use their payment systems, using developer data to compete, and self-preferencing, and would let users install apps outside their stores — directly cutting into their app store commission revenue and gatekeeping power. Their interest in the bill ran against cheaper options for consumers and developers.

Developers would keep more of their revenue by escaping up-to-30% payment mandates and could sue for triple damages if harmed. Most developers are small businesses, so their gains track consumers' gains.
Consumers would see more app choices, the ability to set third-party defaults, and likely lower in-app prices as payment mandates fall away.
